topics.description: Core ideas shared by all programming languages: variables, data types, conditionals, loops, functions, and basic debugging. Once learned, you can break a small problem into steps and write simple working programs.

The Python language itself: indentation-based syntax, lists, tuples, dicts and sets, list comprehensions, def functions, lambda, generators, decorators, classes, try/except, file I/O, import and modules, pip, venv, and the standard library such as os, sys, json, datetime and collections.

JavaScript language syntax and built-ins: let/const/var, hoisting, closures, this, prototypes, ES6 classes, arrow functions, destructuring, spread, template literals, array methods like map/filter/reduce, JSON, ES modules import/export, and DOM manipulation with event listeners.

TypeScript is JavaScript with a static type system. It covers type annotations, interfaces, generics, and compiler configuration, so you can write safer, more maintainable JavaScript and catch bugs before runtime.

The part of JavaScript that deals with code that runs later: callbacks, promises, async/await and the event loop. Once learned, you can fetch data, handle errors and sequence or parallelise asynchronous tasks without blocking.

Java with its static typing and object-oriented design: classes, inheritance, interfaces, abstract classes, ArrayList and HashMap collections, generics, checked exceptions, streams and lambdas, plus the JVM, bytecode, javac, JDK and JRE, and Maven or Gradle builds.

The Go programming language: its syntax, types, structs and interfaces, error handling, goroutines and channels, and standard tooling. Once learned, you can build and test simple command-line tools and network services in idiomatic Go.

A systems programming language focused on memory safety without garbage collection. Covers ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, traits, error handling and Cargo, so you can build fast, reliable command-line tools and services.

Writing queries to retrieve, filter, join, aggregate and modify data in relational databases. Once learned, you can answer questions from tables using SELECT, JOINs, GROUP BY and subqueries, and insert, update and delete records.

PostgreSQL is a specific open-source relational database system built on SQL. Covers installing and administering it, its data types (JSONB, arrays), indexes, query planning, transactions, and extensions, so you can run and tune a Postgres database.

Covers designing relational schemas: modeling entities and relationships, choosing keys, normalizing tables, and using constraints and indexes sensibly. Once learned, you can turn requirements into a clean, consistent database schema.

Covers non-relational data stores such as document, key-value, wide-column and graph databases, and when to choose them over relational ones. A learner can model data for a NoSQL store, run basic queries, and weigh consistency and scaling trade-offs.

Tracking changes to files with Git: committing, branching, merging, resolving conflicts and syncing with remote repositories. Once learned, you can collaborate on code safely and recover from mistakes in a project's history.

Working in a Linux shell: navigating the filesystem, managing files and permissions, using pipes and redirection, and running and scripting basic commands. Once learned, you can operate a Linux machine and automate simple tasks from the terminal.

Covers structuring web pages with semantic HTML and styling them with CSS, including the box model, flexbox, grid and responsive layout. Once learned, you can build and style a responsive static web page from scratch.

Web accessibility is the part of HTML and CSS work focused on making sites usable by people with disabilities. Once you know it, you can apply WCAG guidelines, semantic markup, ARIA, keyboard support and contrast rules, and audit pages with assistive tech.

React's component model for building UIs: JSX syntax, function and class components, props, component state, conditional rendering, lists and keys, event handling, forms, lifting state up, the virtual DOM and reconciliation, and composing component trees in single-page apps.

The hooks API for function components in React: managing state, side effects, context, refs and memoization, and writing custom hooks. Once you know it, you can build and debug stateful function components without classes.

Vercel's full-stack framework with the App Router: file-based routes, layouts, server components and server actions, SSR, SSG and ISR, getServerSideProps, route handlers, middleware, next/image, next/link and deploying on Vercel.

Node.js runtime internals and server tooling: CommonJS and ES modules, require and package.json, npm scripts, the fs, path, http and streams modules, process and Buffer, EventEmitter, Express routes and middleware, and building REST APIs and CLI tools that run on the V8 engine.

How to design clean, consistent web APIs around resources, HTTP methods, status codes, versioning, pagination and error handling. Once learned, you can design and document a RESTful API that other developers can use easily.

A query language and runtime for APIs where clients request exactly the data they need. Covers schemas, types, queries, mutations, resolvers and subscriptions, so you can design and consume a GraphQL API.

Concrete containers for holding data in memory: arrays, linked lists (singly and doubly), stacks, queues, deques, hash tables and collisions, binary search trees, AVL and red-black trees, tries, heaps and priority queues, and graph adjacency lists or matrices. Covers insertion, lookup and deletion costs of each.

Classic algorithm techniques and their running time: quicksort, mergesort, binary search, recursion and divide and conquer, greedy methods, dynamic programming, graph traversal (BFS, DFS), shortest paths such as Dijkstra, and Big O time complexity analysis.

Covers modelling software with classes and objects, including encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction. Once learned, you can design and build programs as collaborating objects and judge when an object-oriented approach fits.

A programming paradigm built on pure functions, immutable data, and composition. Once you know it, you can use map/filter/reduce, closures, and higher-order functions to write predictable code with fewer side effects.

Reusable solutions to common software design problems, such as factory, observer, strategy and decorator. Once you know them, you can recognise recurring problems in a codebase, choose a fitting pattern and apply it without overengineering.

Writing code that is readable and easy to change, and improving existing code safely without altering its behavior. Covers naming, small functions, removing duplication, spotting code smells, and applying common refactoring moves.

Covers the principles and practice of verifying that software works: unit, integration and end-to-end tests, test design, mocking, and coverage. After learning it, you can write reliable automated tests and judge what and how much to test.

The practice of writing a failing automated test before the code, then making it pass and refactoring in small cycles. It narrows software testing to a design workflow; learners can build features incrementally with a reliable test suite.

Writing and reading patterns that match, extract and replace text, including character classes, quantifiers, groups, anchors and lookarounds. Once learned, you can validate input, search logs and transform text in code or editors.

The pandas library for Python, covering Series and DataFrames, loading data, cleaning, filtering, grouping, merging and summarizing tabular data. Once learned, you can analyze and reshape real-world datasets in Python; this narrows Python to data analysis.

Building Docker images from a Dockerfile (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, multi-stage builds, layers and caching), running containers with docker run, bind mounts and volumes, port mapping, bridge networks, docker-compose.yml, and pushing images to Docker Hub.

Kubernetes cluster objects and operations: pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, namespaces, StatefulSets, probes, autoscaling (HPA), rolling updates and Helm charts. Driven through kubectl and YAML manifests, with nodes, the control plane and kubelet.

Covers automating the build, test and release of software with pipelines that run on every change. Once learned, you can set up a pipeline that tests code, builds artifacts and deploys them safely, including basic rollback and secrets handling.

Defining and managing servers, networks and cloud resources through version-controlled code instead of manual setup. Once learned, you can write, review and apply reproducible infrastructure configurations and manage changes safely.

Vendor-neutral cloud models and terms: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS service models, public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud deployment, virtualization and hypervisors, elasticity, scalability, pay-as-you-go pricing, regions and availability zones, and the shared responsibility model.

Amazon's cloud platform and its named services: EC2 instances, S3 buckets, VPC, RDS, DynamoDB, Lambda, CloudFront, Route 53, CloudWatch and IAM users, roles and policies. Covers the AWS console and CLI, regions and availability zones, and deploying and securing apps on AWS.

Covers instrumenting software with metrics, logs and traces, building dashboards and alerts, and using them to detect, diagnose and understand problems in running systems. Learners can set up basic monitoring and investigate incidents.

Covers how computers communicate over networks: the layered models, IP addressing and subnets, TCP and UDP, DNS, routing, and common network devices. Once learned, you can explain how data travels between machines and troubleshoot basic connectivity problems.

The application-layer protocol of the web, a part of computer networking: requests and responses, methods, status codes, headers, caching, cookies and HTTPS. Once learned, you can inspect, debug and reason about web traffic between clients and servers.

Covers how web applications are attacked and defended, including injection, cross-site scripting, CSRF, and insecure configuration. Once learned, you can spot common vulnerabilities and apply standard defenses in a web app.

A part of web application security covering how systems verify who a user is and decide what they may do: password storage, sessions, tokens, OAuth and role-based access. Learners can design and implement secure login and permission checks.

Kernel-level resource management: processes and threads, CPU scheduling, context switches, deadlock, synchronization with mutexes and semaphores, paging and virtual memory, file systems, interrupts, device drivers, system calls, and Linux or Windows internals.

How programs run multiple tasks at once, covering threads, processes, locks, race conditions, deadlocks and common concurrency models. Once learned, you can design and debug code that safely shares work across cores or tasks.

Sizing and architecting large-scale products such as URL shorteners, news feeds or chat apps: capacity estimation, load balancing, caching, sharding and replication, message queues, CDNs, CAP theorem and latency versus throughput trade-offs, as practiced in system design interviews.

Splitting an application into small, independently deployable services, each owning its own data: bounded contexts, API gateway, service discovery, REST/gRPC and message-based communication, saga pattern, circuit breaker, eventual consistency, and migrating a monolith step by step.

How source code is turned into running programs: lexing, parsing, syntax trees, semantic analysis, code generation, and interpretation. Once learned, you can build a simple interpreter or compiler and reason about how language features are implemented.

Designing, building and shipping apps for phones and tablets, covering app structure, screens and navigation, device features, local and remote data, and release to app stores. Once learned, you can build a simple working app for iOS or Android.

Building software that uses large language models through APIs: prompt design, structured outputs, retrieval-augmented generation, tool calling, and evaluation. Once learned, you can design, ship and test a working LLM-powered feature or app.

Manipulating variables and algebraic expressions: simplifying, distributing, factoring polynomials, laws of exponents, radicals, solving linear and quadratic equations (quadratic formula, completing the square), inequalities, absolute value, systems of equations and word problems.

Function notation f(x), domain and range, the vertical line test, plotting and sketching curves on the coordinate plane, intercepts, asymptotes, shifts, stretches and reflections, composite and inverse functions, piecewise and rational functions, and exponential and logarithmic graphs.

Euclidean figures and their measurements: parallel and perpendicular lines, angle pairs, triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA) and similarity, Pythagorean theorem, polygons, circle arcs, chords and tangents, perimeter, area, surface area and volume of prisms, cylinders, cones and spheres, plus two-column proofs.

Sine, cosine, tangent and their reciprocals (SOH-CAH-TOA), the unit circle, radians and degrees, the law of sines and law of cosines, Pythagorean and angle-sum identities, inverse trig functions, solving trig equations, and graphing sinusoids by amplitude, period and phase shift.

Single-variable calculus as a whole: limits and continuity, the derivative and the integral joined by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, with applications like related rates, optimization, area under a curve, and sequences and series such as Taylor series.

Limits and continuity, the limit definition of the derivative, and differentiation rules (power, product, quotient, chain rule, implicit and trigonometric, exponential and log derivatives). Covers tangent lines, related rates, L'Hôpital's rule, the mean value theorem, and max-min and curve sketching.

Antiderivatives and indefinite integrals, Riemann sums, definite integrals, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, u-substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions, trig substitution, improper integrals, area between curves, solids of revolution, arc length, and series convergence tests.

Calculus in two and three dimensions: partial derivatives, gradient, directional derivatives, double and triple integrals, polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, Jacobians, vector fields, line and surface integrals, and Green's, Stokes' and divergence theorems.

Equations involving an unknown function and its derivatives: separable, linear and exact first-order ODEs, integrating factors, second-order equations with constant coefficients, initial value problems, Laplace transforms, direction fields, and growth, decay and mixing models.

Matrices and vectors: Gaussian elimination and row reduction, matrix multiplication and inverses, determinants, span, basis, rank and null space, linear independence, dot product, orthogonality, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization, and SVD.

Sets, relations and functions, mathematical induction, proof techniques such as contradiction and contrapositive, permutations and combinations, the pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion, recurrence relations, modular arithmetic and predicate logic with truth tables and quantifiers.

Vertices and edges, directed and weighted graphs, adjacency lists and matrices, paths, cycles, Euler and Hamilton circuits, spanning trees, BFS and DFS, Dijkstra shortest paths, planar graphs, graph coloring, bipartite matching and network flow.

Covers algorithms for approximating solutions to mathematical problems on a computer, including root finding, interpolation, numerical integration and differentiation, and solving linear systems, along with error and stability. Learners can choose and implement suitable methods and judge their accuracy.

Covers formulating problems as objectives and constraints and solving them: unconstrained and constrained optimization, Lagrange multipliers, linear programming, convexity, and gradient-based methods. Learners can model and solve basic optimization problems.

Sample spaces and events, permutations and combinations, Bayes' theorem, independent events, dice, coin and card problems, binomial, Poisson and normal distributions, expected value and variance of random variables, and the law of large numbers.

Mean, median, standard deviation, histograms and boxplots for summarising data, plus sampling methods, the normal distribution, standard error, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, p-values, t-tests and chi-square tests for drawing conclusions about populations from samples.

The part of statistics that uses sample data to decide whether an observed effect is likely real or due to chance, covering null and alternative hypotheses, p-values, errors and common tests. Once learned, you can pick, run and interpret a test such as a t-test or chi-square.

A part of statistics focused on modeling the relationship between a response and one or more predictors. Once learned, you can fit and interpret linear and logistic regression models, check their assumptions, and use them to explain and predict.

A part of statistics that treats unknown quantities as probability distributions and updates beliefs with data using Bayes' theorem. Once learned, you can specify priors, compute posteriors, and interpret credible intervals and simple Bayesian models.

Classical ML workflow on tabular data: decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, SVMs, k-nearest neighbours, k-means and PCA, with train/test splits, cross-validation, bias-variance, overfitting, regularization, feature engineering, and metrics like precision, recall and ROC AUC.

Multi-layer neural networks trained with backpropagation: activation functions, convolutional networks (CNN), recurrent networks and LSTMs, attention and transformer architectures, plus regularization such as dropout and batch normalization. Frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow, GPU training and image or text models.

Motion of particles and rigid bodies under forces: projectile motion, velocity and acceleration, Newton's second law, free fall, work-energy theorem, conservation of momentum, elastic and inelastic collisions, torque and angular momentum, orbits, springs and pendulums.

Coulomb's law, electric fields and Gauss's law, electric potential, capacitance and dielectrics, magnetic fields and forces, Biot-Savart and Ampère's laws, Faraday's law, Lenz's law, induced EMF, displacement current and Maxwell's equations.

Temperature scales, heat capacity, latent heat, the zeroth, first, second and third laws, entropy, ideal gas law, isothermal and adiabatic processes, Carnot cycle, heat engines, refrigerators, and thermal efficiency, with Boltzmann's microstate view of entropy.

Wavelength, frequency, amplitude, wave speed, standing waves, resonance, the Doppler effect and sound intensity in decibels. Light topics include Snell's law, total internal reflection, thin lenses, mirror equation, ray diagrams, double-slit interference, single-slit diffraction, gratings and polarization.

Covers Einstein's 1905 theory of motion at speeds near light: relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, length contraction, Lorentz transformations and mass-energy equivalence. Learners can solve problems comparing observers in different inertial frames.

Wavefunctions, the Schrödinger equation, operators and eigenvalues, quantized energy levels, spin, uncertainty principle, superposition and measurement collapse. Typical problems: particle in a box, quantum harmonic oscillator, tunneling, hydrogen atom orbitals, bra-ket notation.

Covers the night sky, the solar system, stars and their life cycles, galaxies and the large-scale universe. Once learned, you can explain how celestial objects move and form, interpret basic observations, and read popular astronomy with understanding.

Covers atoms, the periodic table, bonding, stoichiometry, states of matter, solutions, acids and bases, and basic energy changes. Once learned, you can balance equations, do mole calculations, and explain why substances react and behave as they do.

A part of general chemistry covering how fast reactions occur and how reversible reactions reach balance. Learners can write rate laws and equilibrium expressions, use K and Q, and predict how conditions shift a reaction.

The study of carbon-based compounds: functional groups, structure and stereochemistry, and the reaction mechanisms that connect them. Once learned, you can name organic molecules, predict reaction products, and propose simple synthesis routes.

Enzyme kinetics (Michaelis-Menten, Km, Vmax, inhibition), amino acids and protein folding, glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and ATP, beta-oxidation, gluconeogenesis, and the structure of sugars, fatty acids and nucleotides as metabolic molecules.

Cell structure and compartments: plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, cytoskeleton, plus membrane transport, endocytosis, cell signaling, mitosis, meiosis, cell cycle checkpoints, and microscopy and cell culture methods.

Covers how traits are inherited and how genes vary: Mendelian patterns, chromosomes, linkage, pedigrees, mutations and basic population genetics. Once learned, you can predict inheritance outcomes and interpret simple genetic data.

DNA replication with polymerase, helicase and Okazaki fragments, transcription by RNA polymerase, mRNA splicing, ribosomal translation and the genetic code, operons and transcription factors, plus PCR, restriction enzymes, plasmid cloning, gel electrophoresis, CRISPR and sequencing.

Natural selection, adaptation, fitness, genetic drift and gene flow acting on populations over generations. Speciation and reproductive isolation, common descent, homology, fossil and molecular evidence, phylogenetic trees, cladistics, coevolution, and the origin of humans and other lineages.

Covers trophic levels, food chains and food webs, predator-prey and competition dynamics, population growth and carrying capacity, succession, biomes, habitats and niches, biodiversity, and nutrient cycling such as nitrogen and water cycles in ecosystems.

The study of microscopic organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa: their structure, growth, metabolism, genetics and roles in health, disease and the environment. Once learned, you can explain how microbes live and cause infection and how they are controlled.

Organs and organ systems of the human body: bones and muscles, heart and blood circulation, lungs and breathing, digestion, kidneys and urine, skin, immune and lymphatic system, hormone glands, reproduction, plus homeostasis and body-level feedback loops.

Neurons, action potentials, synaptic transmission and neurotransmitters, neural circuits, and brain regions such as cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, cerebellum and basal ganglia. Includes sensory pathways, motor control, synaptic plasticity, neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG) and neural bases of memory and perception.

The study of how diseases and health outcomes are distributed in populations and what causes them. Covers measures of disease frequency, study designs, bias and confounding, and outbreak investigation, so a learner can interpret and critique health studies.

Covers how the Earth is built and how it changes: minerals, rock types, plate tectonics, volcanoes, earthquakes, weathering and geologic time. Once learned, you can read a geologic map, identify common rocks, and explain how landscapes formed.

Covers how Earth's climate system works, including the greenhouse effect, energy balance, carbon cycle, and evidence for past and present climate change. Learners can interpret climate data and explain causes, feedbacks, and projected impacts.

Resistors, capacitors and inductors in networks: Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws, series and parallel combinations, node and mesh analysis, Thevenin and Norton equivalents, superposition, RC and RL transients, and phasor analysis of sinusoidal AC circuits.

Truth tables, Karnaugh maps and Boolean simplification for AND, OR, NAND, NOR and XOR gate networks. Builds adders, multiplexers, decoders, latches, flip-flops, counters, registers and finite state machines, with timing and Verilog or VHDL.

Continuous-time and discrete-time signals, impulse and step functions, impulse response, convolution, Fourier series, Fourier transform, Laplace and z-transforms, sampling, and frequency response and filtering of LTI systems.

Closed-loop feedback design for dynamic systems: block diagrams, plant transfer functions, poles and zeros, step response (rise time, overshoot, settling time), steady-state error, root locus, Bode and Nyquist stability margins, and PID tuning, lead-lag compensators.

Equilibrium of rigid bodies at rest: resultant forces, moments and couples, free-body diagrams, support reactions, truss analysis by method of joints and sections, frames, Coulomb friction, centroids, center of gravity and moments of inertia of areas.

Liquids and gases at rest and in motion: hydrostatic pressure, Archimedes' principle and buoyancy, continuity equation, Bernoulli's equation, viscosity, laminar and turbulent flow, Reynolds number, head loss in pipes, drag and lift, and the Navier-Stokes equations.

Covers how the atomic structure and processing of metals, ceramics, polymers and composites determine their mechanical, thermal and electrical properties. A learner can explain why materials behave as they do and choose suitable materials for a design need.

Preparing and delivering speeches and talks to a live room or webinar: speech outlines, openings and closings, slide deck design, rehearsal, stage fright, voice projection, pacing, eye contact, gestures, podium presence and handling Q&A.

Clear, concise written communication for the workplace: emails, memos, reports and proposals. Once you know it, you can structure a message for its audience and purpose, edit for clarity and tone, and get readers to act.

Narrative structure and technique: three-act structure, hero's journey, inciting incident, conflict, stakes, rising action, climax and resolution, plus character arcs, hooks, show-don't-tell, and anecdotes or business stories that move an audience emotionally.

Covers the craft of writing original fiction, poetry and personal prose, including character, voice, scene, imagery and revision. A learner can draft and polish short stories or poems and give their work a distinct style.

Writing persuasive text for ads, landing pages, emails and product pages that gets readers to act. Once learned, you can write headlines, benefit-led copy and calls to action, and tailor the message to an audience and goal.
The rules of English words, sentences, punctuation and usage. Once learned, you can build clear grammatical sentences, fix common errors, and choose correct forms in writing and speech.

Spanish language: ser vs estar, preterite and imperfect, subjunctive, gendered nouns, rolled r and vowel sounds, tener and hacer idioms, greetings, food and travel phrases, plus Latin American and Castilian usage.

Bargaining over price, pay and terms: setting a BATNA, reservation point and target, finding the zone of possible agreement (ZOPA), anchoring, concessions, trading issues and counteroffers, and closing a deal both parties sign, as in salary, contract or vendor talks.

Selling to buyers: cold calling and outreach, lead generation, qualifying leads, discovery calls, pitching and demos, handling objections, closing, follow-up, and tracking deals through a CRM pipeline and quota.

Serving customers well across phone, email and chat: listening, handling questions and complaints, and recovering from problems. Once learned, you can resolve issues professionally and leave customers satisfied.

Project charters, scope statements and work breakdown structures, Gantt charts, critical path, milestones, project budgets and resource allocation, risk registers, stakeholder communication, change control, and project closure. Covers waterfall-style planning, status tracking and delivery against a deadline.

Scrum framework and Agile values: sprint planning, product and sprint backlogs, daily standups, sprint reviews and retrospectives, user stories, story points, velocity and burndown charts, plus Scrum Master and team roles, Kanban boards and the Agile Manifesto.

Product roadmaps, backlog prioritisation with frameworks like RICE, MoSCoW and Kano, product requirements documents (PRDs), user stories, product vision and strategy, product-market fit, KPIs and OKRs, and go-to-market and launch decisions as a product manager or product owner.

Running research with real users: recruiting participants, writing discussion guides and screeners, moderated and unmoderated usability sessions, contextual inquiry, diary studies, surveys, card sorting, affinity mapping, personas and journey maps built from observed behavior and quotes.

Shaping how a digital product looks, flows and feels: user flows, information architecture, wireframes, mockups, clickable prototypes in Figma, visual hierarchy, layout, navigation patterns, accessibility, design systems and iterating on screens through design critique.

Core principles of visual design: layout, hierarchy, typography, color, contrast, and composition. Once learned, you can create clear, balanced designs such as posters, social graphics, and slides, and critique design choices.

Covers how to use a camera to make deliberate images: exposure (aperture, shutter speed, ISO), focus, light, composition, and basic editing. Once learned, you can shoot well-exposed, well-composed photos in varied conditions and develop a personal style.

Covers the core skills of representational drawing: line control, shape and proportion, perspective, shading and value, and drawing from observation. Once learned, you can sketch objects, scenes and figures with believable form and depth.

The language of Western music: notation, rhythm, scales, keys, intervals, chords and basic harmony. Once learned, you can read simple scores, analyse how songs are built, and use that knowledge to write or arrange music.

Promoting a brand across online channels: paid ads (Google Ads, Meta ads, PPC), social media campaigns, email newsletters and automation, plus campaign goals, conversion funnels, audience targeting, KPIs, analytics dashboards, A/B testing and budget allocation by ROAS and CPA.

Getting pages to rank in Google's organic results: keyword research and search intent, title tags, meta descriptions, headings, internal links, backlinks and link building, crawling, indexing, sitemaps, robots.txt, page speed, Core Web Vitals, schema markup and Search Console audits.

Turning an idea into a new company: customer discovery interviews, problem-solution fit, MVP building, lean canvas, bootstrapping versus venture capital and pitch decks, founder equity, pivoting, and landing the first paying customers.

How organizations choose where to compete and how to win: analyzing industries and competitors, identifying sources of competitive advantage, and shaping positioning and growth choices. Learners can evaluate a company's strategy and propose strategic options.

Covers the core legal concepts behind running a business: contracts, business structures, liability, intellectual property, employment basics and regulatory compliance. Learners can spot common legal risks and know when to seek a lawyer.

Covers how businesses record and summarize financial activity: double-entry bookkeeping, the accounting equation, journals and ledgers, and preparing basic financial statements. Once learned, you can record transactions and produce a simple balance sheet and income statement.

aliases: analyzing balance sheets and income statements
topics.description: Interpreting a company's income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement using ratios and trend analysis. Once learned, you can judge profitability, liquidity, leverage and cash generation and compare firms.

How companies make financial decisions: evaluating investments with NPV and IRR, estimating cost of capital, choosing between debt and equity, and managing working capital. Learners can value projects and judge a firm's financing choices.

Handling your own household money: building a monthly budget, tracking spending, saving for an emergency fund, paying off credit card and student debt, credit scores, filing income taxes, choosing insurance, and setting up retirement accounts like a 401(k) or IRA.

A part of personal finance focused on growing money through assets such as stocks, bonds and funds. Covers risk, return, diversification and fees, so a learner can build and maintain a simple diversified portfolio.

How individuals, households and firms make choices under scarcity and how markets set prices and quantities. Covers supply and demand, elasticity, costs, market structures and market failures, so you can analyze everyday and business decisions.

The study of whole economies: GDP, inflation, unemployment, interest rates, fiscal and monetary policy, and international trade. Once learned, you can interpret economic news and explain how policy choices and shocks affect growth and prices.

Building and using worksheets in Excel or Google Sheets: entering and formatting data, writing formulas and functions, sorting and filtering, charting, and summarizing with pivot tables. Lets you organize, analyze and present everyday data.

Leadership styles and theories (transformational, servant, situational), crafting and communicating a vision, inspiring and influencing others, leading by example, building trust, and developing other leaders and organisational culture.

Running a team as a line manager: one-on-ones, setting goals and expectations, delegating tasks, performance reviews, coaching and career development of direct reports, onboarding new hires, handling underperformance, absence and conflict within the team.

A part of people management focused on delivering specific, constructive feedback and responding well to feedback from others. Once learned, you can prepare and hold feedback conversations that improve performance and keep trust intact.

Covers how to run a fair, effective hiring process: defining a role, sourcing and screening candidates, conducting structured interviews, and making evidence-based offer decisions. Also covers performing well as a candidate in interviews.

Working through disputes between people: finding root causes, separating positions from interests, using active listening and I-statements, calming heated exchanges, and bringing in a neutral mediator. Covers conflict styles, workplace and family disputes, and win-win settlements.

Goleman's model of emotional intelligence: naming and tracking your own feelings, triggers and moods, self-regulation, internal motivation, empathy and social awareness, and reading facial expressions, tone and body language to understand how others feel.

Managing your own days and attention: to-do lists, Eisenhower matrix, time blocking, calendar planning, Pomodoro, batching, saying no, beating procrastination and distractions, and daily or weekly reviews to stay on top of your workload.

Evaluating everyday claims and arguments: identifying premises and conclusions, hidden assumptions, strawman, ad hominem, slippery slope and false dilemma fallacies, cognitive biases, source credibility, correlation versus causation, and telling strong arguments from weak ones.

Frames choices under uncertainty with decision trees, expected value and utility, weighted decision matrices, cost-benefit and regret analysis, pre-mortems, and reversible versus irreversible decisions. Also covers cognitive biases such as anchoring, sunk cost and overconfidence that distort choices.

A broad introduction to how people think, feel, behave and develop, covering major areas such as learning, memory, motivation, personality, social behavior and mental health. Once learned, you can explain key theories and evaluate everyday claims about behavior.

A part of introductory psychology focused on systematic errors in human judgment, such as confirmation bias, anchoring and availability. Once learned, you can spot these biases in your own and others' reasoning and use simple strategies to reduce their effect.

Covers major ethical frameworks such as consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics, and how to apply them to real dilemmas. Once learned, you can analyse moral problems, weigh competing arguments and justify a position clearly.

Human past across continents from prehistory and Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, China and India through medieval kingdoms, the Silk Road, empires, the Renaissance, colonialism, revolutions, industrialization, world wars and the Cold War. Uses dates, primary sources and historiography.

Designing effective learning experiences, from defining learning objectives and assessing learner needs to sequencing content, choosing activities, and evaluating results. Once learned, you can build a course or training program that measurably teaches what it intends to.

Covers how food supplies energy and nutrients, including macronutrients, vitamins, minerals, hydration and energy balance. Once learned, you can read food labels, evaluate common diet claims and plan balanced meals for your own goals.

Covers the principles and practice of building muscular strength and size through resistance exercise, including core lifts, form, progressive overload, programming and recovery. A learner can design and safely follow a basic training plan.

Covers the core practices of mindfulness and meditation, including breath awareness, body scans, open monitoring and loving-kindness. Once learned, you can build a steady daily practice and use it to manage stress and attention.

Core kitchen skills for preparing meals at home: knife work, heat control, basic cooking methods like sautéing, roasting and boiling, seasoning, and following and adapting recipes. Once learned, you can cook balanced everyday meals safely and confidently.
